‘The active smoking of tobacco products, particularly of
cigarettes, is without doubt the biggest single risk factor in
Tung cancer (ARC, 1986). In addition, smoking causes
‘other respiratory diseases and is thought to be a major con
tributing risk for developing cardiovascular disease (US
DHHS, 1983, 1989), On the other hand, the health effects
of environmental tobacco smoke (ETS), a major pollutant
of indoor atmospheres, are defined with less certainty. ETS
is a mixture of mainstream cigarette smoke (MS) that is
exhaled by smokers and of sidestream cigarette smoke (SS),
the smoke rising off the tip of smoldering cigarettes. A re
cent report (US EPA, 1992) clearly described the potential
adverse health impacts of ETS. The conclusions were
mostly based on several epidemiological studies ofanassoci-
ation of exposure to ETS with the development of lung
‘cancer in nonsmokers and with respiratory diseases in chil-
dren,
‘The toxicology and potential carcinogenicity of MS have
‘been examined in numerous experimental studies (LARC,
1986). Such studies may in fact mimic to a certain degree

exposure to ETS, given that the animals were usually ex-
posed in a ciosed space to clouds of cigarette smoke which
they were forced to inhale involuntarily. However, difer-
ences exist between the chemical composition of MS gener-
ated by puffing cigarettes compared to SS emanating from
the glowing tip of a cigarette (Rodgman, 1992). This
warrants a more detailed analysis of the effects of SS on
biological systems, including whole animals.
The effects of SS on the respiratory tract of laboratory
animals have been investigated in only a few studies. Von
Meyerinck et al. (1989) exposed rats and hamsters to SS
(chamber concentration, 4.3 mg/m? of particles) for 90
days and found reversible hyperplasia and metaplasia ofthe
epithelium in the nasal turbinates in rats. More recently
Coggins ef al. (1992) reported a similar effect of SS in a
-day exposure study in rats. Effects were seen only inthe
most rostral part of the nasal cavity of rats exposed to 10
mg/m? of wet total particulate matter, but not following
exposure to lower particle concentrations (1.0 or 0.1 mg/
m)) Furthermore the effects were fuly reversible, The au-
thors suggested that, based on their experiments, 1 mg/m?
represented a NOEL for SS. In this paper we present an
analysis of cell proliferation in the airways and pulmonary
parenchyma of mice exposed to $S at a concentration of
‘mg/m? of total suspended particulate matter.
